meta.blurb: Inside a hidden drawer, furniture restorer Iris finds thirty letters that were written but never sent. To deliver them at last, she must travel to a seaside town, and face the letters she has never sent herself.
meta.bible: Iris Calloway: a furniture restorer in her late twenties, careful and guarded, who keeps a folder of unsent messages. Pia: Iris's sister, who quarrelled with her over their late mother's house. Mr Fenn: the auctioneer who sold the desk. Ruth Ashby: a clever, upright woman of eighty-four, once a girl of nineteen on holiday; she wrote the letters in 1961 to 1963 and hid them in her desk; she never married. Daniel Marsh: Ruth's first love, a clockmaker's son, now in his eighties, patient and kind; he waited at the station and his four letters came back; he later married Margaret, who has died. Margaret: Daniel's late wife. Jonah Marsh: Daniel's grandson, about thirty, a clockmaker, shy and warm. Saltmere: a small windswept harbour town with a white lighthouse. Quay Street: where Marsh and Son clockmakers stands. Marsh and Son: the clock shop. Harbour View: the care home with a rose garden, two hours' drive from Saltmere. Ruth's father: a banker who moved the family to the city. The oak desk: has a hidden space behind a stuck drawer, with letters tied with a blue ribbon. Months and days are named as in the text, from March to late summer. Voice and tone: tender, quiet and hopeful, a gentle love story about saying things out loud, with a happy ending.

B1B2: Iris Calloway restored old furniture for a living, and she loved nothing more than a piece with a secret. That night, in her workshop, she began work on a battered oak desk she had bought at an auction.
One drawer was stuck fast and would not open, however hard she pulled. When she finally eased it out, she saw that the space behind it was strangely shallow, and she reached in.
Inside the hidden space was a bundle of letters tied with a faded blue ribbon. Every envelope was addressed to a man named Daniel, and not one of them had ever been posted.
Iris knew she should not read them, but she was too curious to stop. The first letter began, “Dear Daniel, I am writing this, and I know I will never send it.”
As Iris read on, the letters slowly began to tell a story. In the summer of 1961, a girl named Ruth had danced all night in Saltmere, and her last dance was with a clockmaker's son.
For three weeks they walked along the harbour wall and ate their picnics beside the lighthouse. Daniel taught her how clocks work, and Ruth taught him to whistle every tune she knew.
Ruth's father was a banker, and he did not want his daughter to marry a poor clockmaker's son. In September he moved the whole family to the city, far from the sea.
The last letter was dated two summers after the dance. It ended, “I should have said it all out loud, and now it is too late to know what you would have answered.”
Iris laid the last page on her knee and sat still for a long time. She felt that she had no right to judge Ruth, because she, too, was good at not sending things.
On her phone was a folder of drafts, and the oldest was a message to her sister Pia. It had been sitting there, unsent, for two years, ever since their quarrel over their mother's house.
The next morning Iris telephoned Mr Fenn, the man who had run the auction. He told her that the desk had belonged to a Miss Ruth Ashby, whose niece had sold it when Ruth moved away.
One address appeared on every envelope: Marsh and Son, Quay Street, Saltmere. On Saturday morning Iris caught the early train, with the letters wrapped in a scarf in her bag.
Saltmere turned out to be a small, windy town with a stone harbour and a white lighthouse. Iris stepped off the train and smelled salt and fish and fresh rain at once.
Marsh and Son was still there, a tiny shop on Quay Street with clocks ticking in the window. Behind the counter, a tall man with oil on his fingers looked up from a watch he was mending.

The man introduced himself as Jonah Marsh and listened carefully while Iris explained about the desk and the letters. His grandfather Daniel was in his eighties, he said, and he did not like to talk about the past.
They found Daniel on the harbour wall, where he fed the gulls every afternoon. He was small and straight-backed, with white hair, and he looked at Iris with sharp blue eyes.
Iris took out the bundle and said that the letters were from a girl named Ruth. Daniel went very still, and the bread slipped from his hand and fell onto the stones.

Daniel said that he had waited for Ruth at the station on the day she had promised to visit. She never came, and the four letters he wrote were sent back with a note saying that nobody of that name lived there.
Daniel asked if he might read one, and Iris gave him the first letter. He read it slowly, his lips moving, and by the end he had to wipe his eyes with his sleeve.
Daniel asked the question that none of them could answer, which was whether Ruth was alive. Iris promised that she would find out, and that she would not stop until she knew.
That evening, since the last train had already gone, Jonah took Iris for fish and chips on the harbour wall. They talked until the lighthouse lamp came on, and neither of them wanted to go in.

The next morning Jonah showed her the workshop behind the shop, where dozens of clocks stood waiting for repair. He told her that the secret of his work was patience, and that most things break because somebody hurried.
Iris examined a cracked wooden clock case and showed Jonah how to glue and clamp it. Their hands met over the wood, and neither of them pulled away.
Over tea, Iris admitted that she kept a folder of unsent messages, and showed him the one for her sister. Jonah read it, handed back the phone, and said gently that she should press send.
That afternoon Mr Fenn telephoned with good news, having spoken to Ruth's niece. Ruth Ashby was alive and well in a care home called Harbour View, about two hours' drive from Saltmere.
When Daniel heard, he went home and put on his best jacket. He combed his hair three times, and his hands shook so much that Jonah had to do his tie.

The three of them set off in Jonah's rattling old van, with Iris squeezed in the middle. Daniel sat very straight, staring at the road, and said that he had waited more than sixty years and could manage two more hours.
Harbour View was a pretty old house with a garden that looked out over the water. Daniel stopped on the path and said that he could not go any further without a minute to breathe.
Ruth Ashby sat by a sunny window with a book on her knee, a small woman with silver hair and a straight back. She looked at the stranger with curiosity, and Iris held out the bundle of letters.
Ruth recognised the blue ribbon at once, and her hand flew to her mouth. She laughed and cried together, and said that the drawer had stuck years ago, and that she had stopped hoping to open it.
Ruth asked in a small voice whether Iris knew what had happened to Daniel. Iris smiled and said that he was waiting in the garden, wearing his best jacket.
Daniel appeared in the doorway with his cap in his hands, and for a moment neither of them could speak. Then Ruth lifted her chin and said, “You are sixty years late, Daniel Marsh.”
They sat side by side on the sofa, holding hands as if they had never stopped. Ruth read the last letter aloud, and when she reached the final line, Daniel answered it.
Iris and Jonah left them alone and walked out into the rose garden. Jonah said that he had never seen his grandfather look so young, and Iris found that she could not answer.
Jonah asked quietly what her own letter was waiting for. Iris took out her phone, shortened the old message to four honest lines, and pressed send before her thumb could stop her.

Within a minute, before she could even put it away, her phone buzzed in her hand. Pia had written back, “I miss you too, you idiot, come to dinner,” and Iris laughed out loud and then burst into tears.
Inside, Ruth explained why she had never posted a single letter. She had been too proud and too afraid that he had forgotten her, and Daniel said that he never had.
Ruth took Iris's hand and asked whether she would finish mending the old desk. She wanted it back in her room, she said, because it had kept her secret for so long.

On the long drive home, Daniel fell asleep against the window with a smile on his face. Jonah glanced across at Iris and asked, a little shyly, if she would have dinner with him when she was next in Saltmere.
Back in her workshop, Iris spent three weeks restoring the desk with more care than she had ever given to anything. Every evening, at about seven, her phone rang, and it was always Jonah.

One Saturday Pia came to the workshop with a cake and a nervous face. The sisters hugged for a long time, and then they talked honestly about their mother's house, and for once neither of them shouted.
One evening Jonah arrived in the city with a small clock he had repaired for her wall. He said it was so that she would never lose track of time, and then he took her to dinner.
Over dinner Jonah took an envelope from his pocket and put it on the table. He admitted that he had written it three weeks ago and had very nearly kept it in his pocket forever.
The letter was short, and it said that Jonah had never met anyone who made him want to say things out loud. Iris folded it carefully, stood up, and kissed him in front of the whole restaurant.
At last the desk was finished, and Iris and Jonah carried it into Ruth's room at Harbour View. Daniel was already there, sitting in the armchair as if he had been there for years.
Ruth opened the secret drawer, which now slid smoothly, and found it empty. She said it would not stay empty, because she and Daniel now wrote to each other, and this time every letter was posted.
In the spring Ruth moved to a small cottage in Saltmere, not far from Daniel's house. Her window looked straight out at the lighthouse where she had once picnicked with a boy who could not whistle.

Iris had been visiting Saltmere every weekend, and she had begun to dream about the light in the harbour. When a shop with a large window came up for rent on Quay Street, she took it before she could think twice.
On a golden evening the four of them sat on the harbour wall, eating chips from paper. Ruth leaned her head on Daniel's shoulder and said that she was in no hurry at all.

On her last night in the city, Iris wrote a letter to Jonah and walked it to the red post box on the corner. It would arrive a day after she did, which was foolish, but some letters matter simply because they are sent.
C1C2: Iris Calloway restored old furniture for a living, and on a cold evening in March she stayed late in her workshop, bent over a battered oak desk that she had bought at an auction for far less than it deserved. The wood was dark with a century of polish and scarred by generations of elbows, and it smelled faintly of lavender and dust. Iris ran her thumb along the edge and felt, as she always did with old things, that the desk was waiting to tell her something.

One drawer was stuck fast, and Iris spent half an hour coaxing it with a thin blade and a great deal of patience until it slid out with a long, tired groan. The space behind it was far too shallow, as though the desk had been built with a secret in its belly, and her heart began to beat a little faster. She slipped her hand into the dark gap, and her fingers touched something soft and papery.

Inside the hidden space lay a bundle of letters tied with a faded blue ribbon, more than thirty of them, their envelopes soft as cloth with age. Every one was addressed in the same slanting hand to a man named Daniel Marsh in a place called Saltmere, and not one of them carried a stamp or a postmark. They had been written, folded and hidden, and nobody had ever read them.

Iris told herself that she ought to put them back, and then she unfolded the first one anyway, because the human heart is not built to leave such a thing unread. It began, in a neat and rather determined hand, “Dear Daniel, I am writing this although I know that I will never send it, because if I do not say it to someone, I think I shall burst.” It was dated the ninth of October, 1961.

As Iris read on, the letters slowly began to tell a story, and it was the oldest and sweetest story in the world. In the summer of 1961 a girl named Ruth Ashby, nineteen and on holiday with her parents, had danced all night in the village hall at Saltmere. The last dance had been with a clockmaker's son named Daniel, and Ruth wrote that she knew, before the music ended, that her life had divided in two.

For three golden weeks they walked together along the harbour wall, shared picnics in the shadow of the white lighthouse, and talked about everything under the sun. Daniel taught her how the tiny wheels inside a clock fit together, and Ruth taught him to whistle every tune she knew, though he never learned to do it properly. She wrote that she could still hear his terrible whistling whenever the wind blew from the sea, and that it made her laugh and cry together.

Ruth's father was a banker with firm opinions, and he had no intention of letting his only daughter fall in love with a poor clockmaker's son. At the end of that summer he packed the family into a car, drove them to the city, and told Ruth briskly that Daniel had probably forgotten her already. She wrote that she had sat in the back seat staring at the road behind them until the sea was gone.

The last letter in the bundle had been written in the summer of 1963, two years after the dance, and the paper was spotted where tears had once fallen. In it Ruth admitted that she had written all these pages because she had been too frightened to post even one, too afraid that Daniel's silence would be the answer. “I should have said it out loud,” it ended, “and now I shall never know what you would have said.”

Iris laid the last page on her knee and sat very still amid the sawdust, while the workshop clock ticked and the lamp hummed. She felt an uncomfortable sense of recognition, for she had no right at all to pity a woman who had never posted her feelings, being herself a lifelong expert at keeping things unsaid. The old desk sat in the lamplight like a patient witness that knew her better than she liked.

On her phone Iris kept a folder of drafts, and the oldest one, a message to her sister Pia, had been waiting there for two years, ever since the quarrel over their late mother's house. She had written it, rewritten it, deleted it and written it again so many times that the words had gone smooth, like a pebble that is turned too often in the hand. Every time she reached for the send button, her thumb simply refused.

The next morning Iris telephoned Mr Fenn, the auctioneer, and asked as casually as she could who had owned the desk. He told her, after much rustling of paper, that it had belonged to a Miss Ruth Ashby, whose niece had sent it for sale when the old lady moved out of her house. Iris thanked him, hung up, and began to search the letters for an address that might lead her to the man who had never received them.

Every envelope carried the same address, Marsh and Son, Quay Street, Saltmere, and on Saturday morning Iris caught the earliest train she could find, with the letters wrapped in a scarf at the bottom of her bag. The journey took four hours, and for most of it she watched the fields turn from green to gold to grey as the land sloped down toward the sea. She had no idea what she would say, or even whether the man she was looking for was still alive.

Saltmere turned out to be a small, windswept town of grey stone and bright paint, with a harbour full of bobbing boats and a white lighthouse standing guard at the end of a long wall. Iris stepped off the train into the smell of salt, seaweed and fresh rain, and she understood at once why a nineteen-year-old girl would have remembered this place for the rest of her life. Gulls wheeled overhead and screamed as if they had been expecting her.

Marsh and Son was still there, a narrow shop squeezed between a bakery and a net-maker's, with a hundred clocks ticking in the window in perfect disagreement. Behind the counter, a tall man of about thirty, with oil on his fingers and a magnifying glass pushed up into his dark hair, looked up from the watch he was mending. His eyes were grey and kind, and Iris found, to her annoyance, that she had completely forgotten what she had come to say.

The man introduced himself as Jonah Marsh, and he listened with growing wariness while Iris explained about the desk, the hidden drawer and the bundle of letters in her bag. His grandfather Daniel was in his eighties, he said carefully, and had a way of going quiet whenever the distant past was mentioned, so he would have to be told gently. Then he took off his apron, locked the till, and said that if she was going to disturb the old man's peace, he would at least like to be standing next to him.

They found Daniel at the end of the harbour wall, where he sat every afternoon in the same patched coat, tossing crusts to the gulls and pretending not to enjoy it. He was small and straight-backed, with a cloud of white hair and a pair of sharp blue eyes that took in Iris, her bag and his grandson's worried face in a single glance. Jonah introduced her gently, and the old man nodded as if visitors with mysterious bags were an everyday event.

Iris drew the bundle from her bag, held out the faded blue ribbon, and said quietly that the letters had been written by a girl named Ruth Ashby. For a long moment Daniel did not move at all, and then the crust slipped from his fingers and the gulls descended upon it in a great shrieking cloud that neither of them noticed. He lowered himself onto the wall as though his knees had turned to water, and whispered the name once, slowly, as if he were testing whether it was real.

In a voice that was almost steady, Daniel told them that Ruth had promised to come back the following summer, and that he had stood at the station for a whole day, in his best jacket, watching every train arrive. She never came, and the four letters he wrote to her were all returned, unopened, with a note scrawled across them saying that nobody of that name lived there. In time, he said, he had married a kind woman named Margaret and been happy for forty years, but he had never entirely stopped looking at trains.

Daniel asked, in a hoarse voice, if he might read one, and Iris gave him the first letter with hands that were not quite steady. He read it slowly, his lips moving, with the wind plucking at the page, and when he reached the last line he took off his glasses and wiped his eyes with the back of his sleeve. Jonah, who had never seen his grandfather cry, put an arm around the old man's shoulders and looked carefully out to sea.

Daniel asked, at last, the question that none of them could answer, which was whether Ruth was still alive, and the words seemed to hang over the water like the cry of a gull. Iris did not know, but she told him that Ruth's name had been on the paperwork of the sale only weeks ago, and that this was a good sign. She promised that she would find out, and that she would not stop looking until she had.

That evening, since the last train had long gone, Jonah took Iris to the end of the harbour wall and bought two paper parcels of fish and chips, which they ate with their fingers while the sun went down. They talked about clocks and furniture, about her workshop in the city and his grandfather's silences, and they argued cheerfully about whether vinegar was necessary. By the time the lighthouse lamp began to turn, neither of them could have said how long they had been laughing.

The next morning Jonah showed her the workshop behind the shop, where dozens of clocks in various stages of disassembly lay on trays like patients waiting for surgery, each ticking or about to tick. He explained that the secret of his work was patience, because most things are broken by somebody in a hurry and can only be mended by somebody who is not. Iris, who had spent her career saying almost exactly the same thing about furniture, felt a small shock of delight.

Jonah had a grandfather clock with a cracked wooden case that had defeated him for a year, and Iris, who could not resist a wounded piece of furniture, showed him how to glue and clamp the split so that it would not show. Their hands met over the polished wood, and for a moment neither of them said anything, because the ticking of fifty clocks seemed suddenly very loud. Jonah cleared his throat and asked, in a voice that was almost normal, whether she took her tea with sugar.

Over tea, in a rush of honesty that surprised her, Iris admitted that she kept a whole folder of unsent messages and showed him the oldest, the one meant for her sister. Jonah read it twice, handed the phone back with great care, and said gently that it was a good message and that it was wasted sitting in the dark. Iris said that she would think about it, which they both understood to mean not yet.

That afternoon Mr Fenn telephoned with good news, having spoken to Ruth's niece, who had been astonished to hear that the old desk had given up a secret. Ruth Ashby was alive, he said, as sharp as a tack at the age of eighty-four, and living in a care home called Harbour View, about two hours' drive from Saltmere. Iris wrote the address on the back of her hand, because she could not find any paper and could not bear to wait.

When Daniel heard the news he said nothing at all, but went home, put on his best jacket and a tie that had not been worn since a funeral, and combed his white hair three times in the hall mirror. His hands shook so much that Jonah had to fasten the tie for him, and neither of them mentioned it. Pausing at the door, the old man asked whether he looked all right, and his grandson said that he looked like a man going to meet his future.

The three of them set off in Jonah's rattling old van, with Iris squeezed between the two men and the faded blue ribbon in her lap, and the coast road unrolled before them like a long grey ribbon of its own. Daniel sat bolt upright, staring through the windscreen, and said that he had waited more than sixty years and could manage two more hours. Then, to everybody's surprise, he began to talk about the dance, the paper lanterns, the smell of the sea, and the way a girl in a yellow dress had laughed at his jokes.

Harbour View turned out to be a pretty, rambling old house with a rose garden that sloped down toward a pale and glittering sea. Halfway up the path Daniel stopped, took a long breath, and said that his legs had suddenly become the legs of a very young and frightened man. Iris squeezed his arm and said that she would go in first, and that he should wait here in the sun.

Ruth Ashby was sitting by a sunny window with a book open on her knee, a small, upright woman with silver hair and the air of someone who had always been the cleverest person in the room. She regarded the stranger with polite curiosity, and Iris, who had rehearsed a speech all the way from Saltmere, forgot every word of it. She simply held out the bundle of letters, with its faded blue ribbon, and said that she had found them in a desk.

Ruth recognised the blue ribbon at once, and her hand flew to her mouth, and her eyes, which were the same clear grey as the sea outside, filled and overflowed. She laughed and cried together and explained that the drawer in her old desk had stuck years ago, and that she had long since stopped hoping she would ever open it again. Then she took the letters in both hands and held them against her chest, as if they might fly away.

Ruth asked, in a small voice that did not sound at all like the cleverest person in the room, whether Iris happened to know what had become of Daniel Marsh. Iris smiled and told her that he was waiting in the garden, wearing his best jacket and an expression of terror, and that he had been waiting there, in one way or another, for most of his life. Ruth stood up so quickly that her book fell off her knee and nobody bothered to pick it up.

Daniel appeared in the doorway with his cap crushed in both hands, and for a long moment the two of them simply looked at each other across more than sixty years, while the clock on the wall ticked and the sea sighed against the rocks. Then Ruth lifted her chin, in exactly the way he remembered, and said, “You are late, Daniel Marsh.” Daniel began to laugh, and then he began to cry, and then he crossed the room in four steps.

They sat side by side on the small sofa, holding hands as if there had been no gap in the years at all. Ruth read the last of her letters aloud in her clear, teacherly voice, and when she came to the line that said she should have said it out loud, Daniel answered before she could finish. “You have said it now,” he told her, “and I heard every word.”

Iris and Jonah tiptoed out and left the two of them alone, and they walked together into the rose garden where the late sun was turning every petal to gold. Jonah said, in a thick voice, that he had never seen his grandfather look so young, and Iris found that she could not answer, because her own throat had closed. They stood side by side on the path, not quite touching, and watched the lit window as if it were a stage.

Jonah asked, very quietly, what her own letter was waiting for, and the question went through Iris like a clear bell. She took out her phone, deleted two years of careful words, wrote only that she was sorry and that she missed her sister, and pressed send before her thumb could argue. Then she stood in the roses with her heart thumping, certain that she had just done the bravest thing of her life, and slightly sick.

Within a minute, before she had even put the phone away, it buzzed in her hand, and the name on the screen was Pia. The reply was only nine words long, “I miss you too, you idiot, come to dinner,” but it undid two years of silence in the time it takes to draw a breath. Iris laughed out loud, then burst into tears, and Jonah, without a word, handed her a clean handkerchief that smelled faintly of clock oil.

When Iris and Jonah came back in, Ruth was explaining, with the frank honesty of the very old, why she had never posted a single letter. She had been too proud to write into a silence, she said, and too frightened that Daniel had moved on, and so she had put her whole heart into a drawer instead of an envelope. Daniel, holding her hand, replied that he had thought of her on most days for sixty years, and that he did not intend to waste a single one of the days that were left.

Ruth took Iris's hand in both of hers and asked whether she would finish restoring the old desk, and bring it to her new room when it was done. She wanted it back, she said, not for the writing, but because it had kept her secret faithfully for sixty years, and a thing that loyal ought not to be left in an auction room. Iris, who had been about to offer, said that she would think of nothing else.

On the long drive back, Daniel fell asleep against the window with his cap in his lap and a smile on his face that did not fade even when the van went over a pothole. Jonah glanced across at Iris in the glow of the dashboard lights and asked, a little shyly, whether she might be persuaded to have dinner with him the next time she came to Saltmere. Iris said that she thought she could probably be persuaded, and then she looked out at the dark sea to hide her grin.

Back in her workshop, Iris spent three weeks restoring the desk with more tenderness than she had ever given to a piece of furniture, easing out every scratch, feeding the dry wood with wax and polishing the old brass handles until they glowed like small suns. Every evening at about seven her phone rang and it was always Jonah, who wanted to know how the desk was getting on and stayed to talk about everything else. She began to notice that she was watching the clock from about half past six.

One Saturday Pia arrived at the workshop with a lemon cake and the nervous face of a person who has rehearsed an apology in the car. The sisters hugged for so long that the cake nearly fell, and then they sat on upturned crates and spoke honestly about their mother's house, her old garden and everything that grief had made them say to each other. For once neither of them shouted, and when Pia left she said that it was the first talk about the house in two years that had not ended with a slammed door.

One evening, without warning, Jonah appeared in the doorway of the workshop holding a small walnut clock that he had spent a fortnight repairing in secret. He hung it on her wall himself, wound it, and said that it was so she would never lose track of the time, which was not at all what his face was saying. Then, since she was covered in sawdust and he was covered in nerves, they went out to find the nearest decent restaurant.

Over dinner Jonah took a crumpled envelope from his inside pocket and laid it on the table between the candle and the bread basket, looking as though it might explode. He confessed that he had written it three weeks ago, after the first phone call, and had very nearly kept it in his pocket for the rest of his life. Iris, who understood better than anyone what it cost him, opened it with great care and read it twice.

The letter was short and plain, and it said that Jonah had never in his life met anyone who made him want to say things out loud, and that he hoped she might feel, a little, the same. Iris folded it along its creases, put it carefully into her pocket, close to her heart, and then she stood up, walked around the table, and kissed him in front of the entire astonished restaurant. Somebody at the next table began to clap, and somebody else asked for the bill.

At last the desk was finished, its oak glowing like honey and its brass handles polished, and Iris and Jonah carried it between them into Ruth's room at Harbour View. Daniel was already there, sitting in the armchair by the window with a newspaper he was not reading, because he had visited every Saturday since the day they had met again. Ruth ran her hand along the wood and said that it looked better than the day she had first sat down to it.

Ruth pulled open the secret drawer, which now glided out as smoothly as silk, and found it empty, which seemed to please her enormously. It would not stay empty for long, she announced, because she and Daniel had begun writing to each other every week, though they were only two hours apart, and this time every single letter was posted. Daniel, looking pleased with himself, said that the postman had started to whistle on his round.

In the spring Ruth moved into a small whitewashed cottage in Saltmere, a short walk from Daniel's house, with a window that looked straight out to the lighthouse where she had once picnicked with a boy who could not whistle. Her old desk stood beneath that window, its secret drawer full of fresh paper and its surface scattered with letters addressed, in two different hands, to people who were now only a few streets apart. Daniel carried her suitcase up the path and refused to let anyone help him.

By midsummer Iris had been visiting Saltmere every weekend for months, and she had begun to dream about the way the light fell across the harbour in the early morning. When a shop with a wide window and a high ceiling came up for rent on Quay Street, she signed the lease on the spot, because a restorer, she told herself sternly, needs good light. Jonah, who was standing beside her, said nothing at all, and then lifted her clean off her feet.

On a golden evening in late summer the four of them sat in a row along the harbour wall, eating chips from paper and watching the lighthouse lamp begin its slow turning. Ruth leaned her silver head on Daniel's shoulder and said that after sixty years of waiting she was in no hurry whatever, and that the sunset could take as long as it liked. Iris looked at the three people beside her and realised that, for the first time in her life, she did not wish to be anywhere else.

On her last night in the city, with the workshop swept and the van packed, Iris sat at the empty bench and wrote Jonah a letter, the first she had ever finished for someone she loved. She walked it to the red post box on the corner, held it above the dark mouth for a long moment, and then let it go, listening to the soft sound of it falling. It would arrive a day after she did, which was perfectly foolish, but she had learned from a stranger's drawer that some words are worth nothing until they are sent.
